slides.say: A semicircle has center K and radius r. M and N lie on its curved boundary, and angle K M N is sixty degrees. What is the ratio of the perimeter of the semicircle to the perimeter of triangle K M N?

So they ask for the perimeter of the semicircle, divided by the perimeter of the triangle. [short pause] There's a shape inside a circle here. We call these inscribed and circumscribed questions, and they're common at the end of the section.
at: So they ask for the perimeter

slides: What do we do in them? We write the lengths of both shapes with the radius of the circle. We'll solve it three ways, the math way, by plugging in a number, and by estimation.

slides.say: [short pause] The math way first. K M and K N are radii, so each one is r. So the triangle is at least isosceles, and its base angles are equal.
at: K M and K N are radii

slides.say: The angle at M is sixty, so the angle at N is sixty too. That leaves sixty for the angle at K. An isosceles triangle with a sixty-degree angle is equilateral, so M N is r too.
at: the angle at N is sixty
so M N is r too

slides.say: So the perimeter of the triangle is r plus r plus r, three r.
Now the semicircle. A lot of students take half of the circumference. That's only partly right. The perimeter has two parts, the curved part on top and the straight line at the bottom.
The curved part is half of the circumference. The circumference is two pi r, and half of it is pi r.
The straight line is the diameter, two radii, so it's two r. So the perimeter of the semicircle is pi r plus two r.
at: The straight line is the diameter
So the perimeter of the semicircle

slides.say: Now we divide, pi r plus two r, over three r. In the top, take r out as a common factor, so it's r times, in brackets, pi plus two. Now r is multiplied on the top and on the bottom, so we cancel it. We get pi plus two, over three. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now the way I recommend for almost everyone, plugging in a number. Instead of the letter r, we pick an easy number for the radius, and we solve with numbers. Then we put the same number into the choices, and the right choice gives the same value. It saves us the algebra mistakes.
The easiest number is one, so the radius is one. K M and K N are one, and the triangle is equilateral, so M N is one too. The triangle's perimeter is three.
The semicircle has a curved part, half of two pi, which is pi. And the diameter is two. So the ratio is pi plus two, over three.
at: So the ratio is pi plus

slides.say: Now we put r equals one into the choices. Choice number one is pi over three, and that's different, so it's out. But in choices two, three and four, multiplying or dividing by one changes nothing. All three give pi plus two, over three.

slides: That's a tie, so one isn't a good number here. We need another number to break the tie, so let's take r equals two.

slides.say: The triangle is two, two and two, so its perimeter is six. The curved part is half of two pi times two, so it's two pi. The diameter is four. So the ratio is two pi plus four, over six. Divide the top and the bottom by two, and it's pi plus two, over three.
at: The triangle is two, two and two

slides.say: Now r equals two in the choices. Choice number two divides by three r, which is six, so it's pi plus two over six. That's half of our value, so it's out. Choice number four multiplies by r, so it's twice our value. It's out too.
Only choice number three gives pi plus two, over three. Choice number three again.
[pause] And the third way, estimation. Say the radius is one again. The triangle is equilateral, so each of its sides is one, and its perimeter is three.
at: Say the radius is one again

slides.say: Now the curved part. The radii to M and N cut it into three arcs. Under each arc there's a straight line of length one, because the three small triangles at K are all equilateral, with sixty degrees each.
And a straight line is the shortest way between two points. So each arc is a bit longer than one. Let's write one plus.
So the curved part is a bit more than three. Add the diameter, two, and the semicircle is a bit more than five. The triangle is three. So the ratio is about five plus, over three.
Choice number one, pi over three. Pi is less than four, so this is less than four over three. We need more than five over three, so it's out.

[pause] Choices two and four have r in them. They're interesting distractors. If r were two, choice number two would be pi plus two over six. If r were three, it would be pi plus two over nine. The ratio would keep changing.
But look. Here's the same figure, and next to it the same figure twice as big. Every length is twice as long, so both perimeters are twice as big.

The semicircle goes from pi plus two to two pi plus four, and the triangle goes from three to six. When we divide, the two cancels. So when we make the figure bigger or smaller, the ratio doesn't change.

So when they ask for a perimeter over a perimeter, or an area over an area, the radius must cancel. Any choice with r in it is a distractor, and it's out at first glance. Choice number two and choice number four are out.

slides: Careful, that's only for the same kind of thing. In an area over a perimeter, an r can stay, because an area has r squared and a perimeter has only r.

slides.say: Choice number three is pi plus two, over three. Pi plus two is a bit more than five, so it's about five plus over three, just what we estimated. Choice number three again. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
